lessons.title: Batch jobs and sbatch
lessons.summary: Write the job down once, hand it to Slurm, and walk away.

blocks.text: An interactive session (srun --pty bash) is good for trying things. Real work, like designing 1,000 sequences or folding 50 structures, takes hours, and you don't want to sit and watch. Instead you write a job script and submit it as a batch job: Slurm queues it, runs it when resources are free, writes everything it prints to a log file, and frees the GPU when it finishes. You can log out in the meantime.

example.out:
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mpnn
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out

module load anaconda
conda activate proteinmpnn
python /opt/ProteinMPNN/protein_mpnn_run.py --pdb_path inputs/target.pdb --out_folder outputs/
example.note: The `#SBATCH` lines at the top are requests to Slurm, written as options. To bash they are just comments. Below them come the commands the job runs, exactly as you'd type them.

command.name: sbatch
command.what: Submits the script as a batch job and prints its job ID: `Submitted batch job 48213`. The job runs later, on its own.

command.name: squeue
command.what: Shows your jobs that are waiting or running. The ST (state) column says PD (pending, waiting for resources) or R (running). A finished job drops off the list.

lessons.title: Cancelling jobs and checking finished ones

command.name: scancel
command.what: Stops a job, waiting or running. Use it when you submitted the wrong thing, so it doesn't hold a GPU for nothing.

try.text: You submitted a job by mistake. Find its ID and cancel it.

command.name: sacct
command.what: Lists your recent jobs, including finished ones, with their final State: COMPLETED, FAILED, TIMEOUT, OUT_OF_MEMORY or CANCELLED. squeue forgets a job once it ends; sacct remembers.

command.name: seff
command.what: For a finished job: how much of the requested memory and time it actually used. Use it to size the next request.

quiz.q: Your job vanished from squeue. Where do you check whether it worked?
quiz.why: Finished jobs leave the queue. sacct shows the final state, and the slurm-JOBID.out log shows the details.

lessons.title: Running programs: htop, ps and kill
lessons.summary: See what is running on the server, and stop a program that isn't a Slurm job.

blocks.text:
Every program running on Geiss-01 is a process: your login shell, a Python script, each program inside a Slurm job. The system gives every process a number, its PID (process ID). Slurm jobs have a different number, the JOBID.

Two numbers, two tools. A Slurm job is stopped with `scancel JOBID`, which stops everything in the job and gives its GPUs and memory back. A program you ran yourself, straight from the command line (for example `python score.py &`, or something you left running and forgot), is not a Slurm job. squeue doesn't list it and scancel can't touch it. You find it with `htop` or `ps` and stop it with `kill PID`.

command.name: htop
command.what: A live table of processes, busiest first, under bars for CPU and memory. The columns that matter: PID, USER (whose process it is), CPU%, MEM%, and Command. It redraws every couple of seconds until you press q. Arrow keys pick a row, and F9 (or k) sends the highlighted process a kill signal. `top` is the older version and is on every Linux machine.

command.name: ps
command.syntax: ps   |   ps ux   |   ps aux | grep python
command.what: Prints the process list once. Plain `ps` shows only what you started from this terminal. `ps ux` shows all of your processes, and `ps aux` shows everyone's, which is handy with `grep`.

example.out:
USER         PID %CPU %MEM    VSZ   RSS TTY      STAT START   TIME COMMAND
student    30408  0.0  0.0  21059 10486 ?        S    14:42   0:00 sshd: student@pts/0
student    30412  0.0  0.0  15029  5243 pts/0    Ss   14:42   0:00 -bash
student    32410 99.8  6.1 14003421 12163481 ?   R    Nov06 1097:12 python score_designs.py
student    40006  0.0  0.0  13823  4194 pts/0    R    14:46   0:00 ps ux
example.note: The python row is the problem: 99.8% CPU since yesterday. Its PID is 32410. `-bash` is your own login shell; leave it alone.

command.name: kill
command.stands: send a signal to a process
command.what: Plain `kill` asks the program to stop (the TERM signal), so it can save and clean up. If the program ignores that and is still listed, `kill -9` forces it to stop at once. `kill %1` stops background job 1 from `jobs`.

flags: Forces it. The program can't save anything, so use it only when plain kill didn't work.
The first background job that `jobs` lists, instead of a PID.

try.text: Start a program in the background, find it, and stop it.

tasks.text: Run `sleep 600 &` (a program that waits ten minutes)

try.hint: sleep 600 &, then ps, then kill PID (or kill %1)

blocks.warn: You can only kill your own processes; anyone else's gives "Operation not permitted". Check the USER column before you kill. And if a program belongs to a Slurm job, use scancel, not kill: killing the job's processes just makes the job fail.

blocks.tip: `pgrep -a python` lists your Python processes with their PIDs, and `pkill -f score.py` kills by name. Run the pgrep version first so you know exactly what pkill will hit.

quiz.q: squeue --me shows your job 48213 running, and you want it stopped. What do you type?
quiz.why: 48213 is a Slurm JOBID, so scancel is the tool. kill takes a PID, which is a different number.

quiz.q: You ran `python plot.py &` on Geiss-01 without Slurm, and it hung. How do you stop it?
options: Find its PID with ps or htop, then kill PID
quiz.why: It isn't a Slurm job, so squeue and scancel don't know about it. Find the PID and kill it; use kill -9 only if plain kill doesn't work.

lessons.title: Why jobs fail
lessons.summary: The three classic failures, how to recognize them, and the fix.

blocks.text: When a job ends badly, check `sacct` for the State and `tail` the log for the last message. Most failures are one of three, and each comes from a request that was too small.

flags: log says no CUDA GPUs / no GPU detected
State TIMEOUT; log stops mid-run, 'DUE TO TIME LIMIT'
Raise --time (check how far it got first)
State OUT_OF_MEMORY; log ends with 'oom-kill' or 'Killed'
Raise --mem; seff shows what it used

try.text: `design.sh` failed in seconds. Read its request lines and its log to see why.

lessons.title: Quick jobs with --wrap
lessons.summary: Submit one command as a batch job without writing a script.

blocks.text: For a single command, writing a script is overkill. `sbatch --wrap="COMMAND"` wraps the command in a script for you. Add any other options as usual.

example.note: -J is short for --job-name. The quotes keep the whole command, pipe included, together as one option.

try.text: Submit `ls inputs` as a job named `peek`.

quiz.q: Why must the command after --wrap= be in quotes when it contains a pipe?
options: Without them, the shell runs the pipe itself before sbatch sees it
quiz.why: The shell would split the line at | and pipe sbatch's own output into wc. Quotes hand the whole command to sbatch.

lessons.title: Many inputs: arrays and dependencies
lessons.summary: One script for many targets, and jobs that wait for other jobs.

blocks.text: An array job runs the same script many times, once per task number. Inside each task, `$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` holds its number, which the script uses to pick its input.

example.note: Task 3 reads line 3 of targets.txt. squeue shows the tasks as JOBID_1, JOBID_2, and so on.

flags: Run tasks 1 to 4, each as its own job with its own GPU
50 tasks, at most 5 running at once
Wait until job 48215 finishes successfully, then start
